rv.q: This show is a laugh-a-minute feast.
By the end of the titular opening number, I was all in.
The first half erupts like a shaken bottle of prosecco, fizzing and flowing with astute hit after hit.
This zesty, in-jokey, crackerjack entertainment proves they’re certainly not one-hit wonders.
It is all amusing though rather familiar and fleeting, the scenes not quite joining up with each other.
But ultimately Moss and Marlow’s rambling tribute to their own friendship seems unlikely to have the staying power of its predecessor: a curio, not a classic.
Why Am I So Single? isn’t in the same league.

Where Six’s 80-minute runtime meant it could get away without having much of a story, this two-and-a-half-hour show definitely sags – its endless callbacks and in-jokes are no substitute for a satisfying storyline.
It is this very nature of respect and playfulness which runs throughout WHY AM I SO SINGLE? and which will guarantee its success among theatregoers who love the musicals and comedy genres.
Its energy and bravery spring from its wild inventiveness.
Why Am I So Single? is a fantastic show with touching moments of friendship, lots of laughs, and exciting song and dance numbers.
Why Am I So Single? feels somewhat flabby.
In many ways, this might be exactly the show a too often overly cautious West End needs right now and the energy in the house was good evidence for that conclusion.
This unabashedly crowd-pleasing — though ultimately somewhat vacuous — show goes all in on relatability and schmaltz, carrying a peppy message about friendship and self-care.
What they fail to do is write a taut or convincing book to elicit that.

It’s a phenomenally powerful rug-pull, in a show that presents itself as a frothy look at how modern is dating is awful, to include one of the most emotionally devastating musical theatre numbers of recent times.
It's uplifting, hilarious, and creative, and an exciting addition to the West End.
Why Am I So Single? is a very fun watch, with bop after bop.
Six creators Toby Marlow and Lucy Moss return with a fun and relatable musical boasting a strong collection of numbers, but an incredibly thin plot holding them all together.
The results prove frustratingly inconsistent with varying elements failing to marry up.
However, in its current form it tries to hard to do too many things and sometimes clumsily fails to connect.
It’s funny, and often clever, yet at its core the plot feels weak.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this follow-up to Six, praising its catchy songs and whip-smart humor about modern dating, but many find it overly self-indulgent and flabby compared to its predecessor's laser-sharp focus.
